question: m01
q: Are real wages going up? Compare wage growth from the ABS Wage Price Index with inflation.

transcript.answer:
**No. Real wages have been falling since late 2025.** Wages are growing at about 3.2% a year, but prices are rising at about 4%.

**Latest figures**
- **Wages:** The ABS Wage Price Index (WPI) rose **3.2%** in the year to the **June quarter 2026** (seasonally adjusted, total hourly pay excluding bonuses). Private sector wages rose 3.1% and public sector wages 3.4%. The September quarter figure isn't out yet.
- **Prices:** Inflation (CPI) was **about 4.0%** in the June quarter 2026. I worked this out from the monthly index, comparing the average of April–June 2026 with April–June 2025. The latest monthly figure, for **August 2026**, is also **4.0%**. The Reserve Bank's preferred underlying measure (trimmed mean) is 3.6%, which is also above wage growth.
- **Real wages:** roughly **−0.8% a year** as of the June quarter 2026.

**How it's moved** (annual % change)

| Quarter | WPI | CPI | Real wage gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 2023 | 4.3 | 4.1 | +0.2 |
| Q2 2024 | 4.1 | 3.8 | +0.3 |
| Q4 2024 | 3.2 | 2.4 | +0.8 |
| Q2 2025 | 3.4 | 2.1 | **+1.3** |
| Q3 2025 | 3.3 | 3.2 | +0.1 |
| Q4 2025 | 3.4 | ~3.7* | −0.3 |
| Q1 2026 | 3.2 | ~4.0* | −0.8 |
| Q2 2026 | 3.2 | ~4.0* | **−0.8** |

*The ABS stopped publishing the quarterly CPI after September 2025, so I calculated these from monthly index averages. They may differ slightly from figures published elsewhere.

**What this means**
- Real wages fell through 2022–23, when inflation peaked at about 7%. They recovered from late 2023 to mid-2025 as inflation dropped faster than wage growth, peaking at about +1.3% in the June quarter 2025.
- Since then wage growth has stayed at about 3.2–3.4%, while inflation picked up again to 3.7–4.6% between late 2025 and 2026. That turned real wage growth negative again from the December quarter 2025.
- With CPI still at 4.0% in August 2026, the September quarter WPI (due in November) would need a big jump to stop the fall. That looks unlikely given wage growth has been slowing.

**One thing to keep in mind:** the WPI tracks the price of a fixed set of jobs, so it leaves out pay rises from promotions or changing jobs. Measures of average earnings can show a somewhat stronger result.
